posts.cooked:
Hi! I run two independent pet shops in the UK. We use Shopify POS and Sumtracker, and buy from around 100 suppliers. Two things eat a lot of time:

1. invoices and repricing

When stock arrives, we manually check each invoice line against the cost in Shopify. If a price has gone up, we work out the new retail price to hold our margin, update Shopify, tell both shops, and print new shelf labels, It’s v slow/mnaual and price rises slip through.

2. Comparing suppliers

Most suppliers want orders through their portals, promotions arrive by email, website or rep, and we have to hit minimum order quantities. In practice, we often just stick with the usual supplier because comparing/optimising takes too long

How do you handle these? Any tools or workflows that actually work with lots of suppliers and multiple locations, or is it spreadsheets for everyone?
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

The first part is the one I’d sort out first, because that’s where a missed price rise quietly eats your margin.

What works for me is matching the invoice lines to the Shopify catalogue by SKU before anything gets updated, so you end up with a short list of just the lines where the cost actually changed — old cost, new cost, and what the retail price needs to be to hold your margin. Anything that doesn’t match a SKU goes on a separate list of its own, so it doesn’t get skipped without anyone noticing.

Two things worth watching: only update the variants that are in the file and leave the rest of the product alone — an overwrite-style import can wipe variants that weren’t in the file. And if your retail price is a fixed margin on cost, work that out in the same pass, so the shelf labels and the till prices both come from the one updated list.

The supplier comparison is a different problem, really — mostly about getting everyone’s prices into one sheet in the first place, which is hard when they all live in separate portals.

FyreTrail can solve those issues for you from what I’m reading. Here’s how:

  1. Invoices and Repricing - When stock arrives you mark what you received. However, you can also see what it was that you ordered and how much the agreement was for. Should you need to change that, you can easily. Because FyreTrail works off of your pre-set margin, retail prices are suggested (* not set - you must confirm it first) for you so you don’t have to do any calcs. Once it arrives, if the Cost of the product rose to a point that your margins are no longer valid, FyreTrail warns you and prevents syncing to Shopify until you’ve reviewed the retail price. The only time you spend is inspecting and confirming. Then, once you mark the PO as received it will automatically sync to Shopify with the data you have updated and confirmed and fully protects your margins with minimal interaction.
  2. Comparing Suppliers - There’s two parts to this that FyreTrail solves:
    1. If you have to order through another portal, FyreTrail offers a few ways to handle this:
      1. Simply read the portal directly using our Chrome browser extension. If your portal is configured it will simply read the page and transpose the purchase order from their portal and create an equivalent purchase order in FyreTrail. If it’s not configured talk to us and we can likely work something out.
      2. Export a PDF from the portal and import that PDF into FyreTrail. We use AI to understand the PDF and import as a purchase order into FyreTrail. It does a remarkable job doing this and handles the external portal really well.
    2. Once you create a Purchase Order and add line items to a PO manually, FyreTrail will tell you if there’s a better deal from another supplier based on purchase history or associated product purchase price. So long as you update those specific products you get in email, website or rep, etc. FyreTrail will recognize these prices as more advantageous to you and suggest you change to the cheaper supplier to take advantage of that price. I do see an opportunity to improve this with what you’re saying so maybe we could coordinate on this to improve the price beating functionality? Minimum order quantities are also trackable in FyreTrail by supplier/product and variant associations. If you ever order from that supplier, those minimums will be enforced if you have them entered.

Sorry for the wordy explanations, but these are not simple topics. The good news is that you have a solution waiting for you.

posts.cooked: Managing costs across 100 suppliers sounds like a lot of work, especially when prices keep changing. I’m curious, are you currently using Shopify mainly for POS and inventory, or do you also manage your full ecommerce store through it?
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

Two shops and 100 suppliers is exactly where checking every invoice line stops being realistic.

Check only what moved. Keep the last cost you paid per SKU, per supplier, and when an invoice arrives compare it against that instead of reading every line. Most lines on a delivery haven’t changed. So you end up looking at five or six rows, not sixty. Add a small threshold, 2% is fine, or a penny of rounding will send you hunting.

Reprice from a floor, not from every rise. Set a minimum margin per category, since food usually runs thinner than toys and accessories, and only reprice when a new cost pushes an item below its floor: new retail = new cost ÷ (1 − target margin), rounded to your usual price ending.

Then batch it once a week. One list, one bulk edit in Shopify, labels printed only for what’s on that list. If both shops use the same Shopify price, the change reaches both tills at once and the list doubles as the note to the other shop.

The supplier comparison is the harder half.

Don’t try to compare everything. Ask your main suppliers for a price list spreadsheet each month and compare your top 50 sellers only, because that’s where the money is. MOQs get easier too when each supplier has a fixed order day.

Disclosure: we’re the developers of Binly. It flags when the same item from the same supplier comes in at a different price than last time, or when an invoice doesn’t add up to its order. It also compares a supplier’s new price list with the previous one and prints shelf labels for exactly what arrived. It won’t change your retail prices for you. That call stays yours.

posts.cooked:
The comparison part gets a lot easier once every invoice line is put into the same terms as your cost in Shopify before you check it. Three things cause most of the false “price went up” alarms (and hide the real ones among them):

  1. Cases vs units. If a supplier invoices per case of 12 and your Shopify cost is per unit, divide first. Note each item’s pack size once so you don’t work it out every time.
  2. VAT. Some invoices show prices with VAT, some without. Keep your Shopify cost ex-VAT (if you’re VAT-registered) and compare ex-VAT only.
  3. Supplier codes. Many invoices use the supplier’s own code, not your SKU. Keep their code against each variant (a metafield works; not the barcode field, since your tills scan that) so lines match without guesswork.

Once lines are like-for-like, the “only look at what moved” approach above works well: with ~100 suppliers you’re checking a handful of lines per delivery, not every one.

Disclosure: I’m working on a receiving tool for this, but everything above works fine with a spreadsheet.

Hi @WB-LS, one thing nobody has mentioned yet: Shopify admin now has its own purchase orders (Products > Purchase orders), and you can receive the stock in POS at each shop.

Since June, a purchase order fills each line with the last price you paid or the product’s cost per item, and you can import the invoice lines by CSV. So the old cost is already sitting next to the new one when a delivery comes in, and the rises are easy to spot.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
A UK retailer with two pet shops, Shopify POS, Sumtracker and roughly 100 suppliers wants to reduce manual invoice checks, catch cost increases, update retail prices and shelf labels, and compare suppliers despite separate ordering portals and minimum-order requirements.

Suggested workflows include matching invoice lines to product SKUs, comparing only changed costs, and checking that pack sizes, VAT treatment and supplier codes are consistent. Several replies recommend setting category-specific minimum margins, calculating revised prices when costs breach those thresholds, and applying changes in batches; one cautions that imports should update only included variants. Shopify purchase orders can also import invoice lines by CSV and show previous costs, but receiving stock does not automatically update product costs.

Two app developers describe tools for invoice comparisons, supplier-price checks and label printing; one also claims to support purchase-order imports and margin-based price suggestions. These are product recommendations, not independently verified outcomes. No workflow was selected, and the retailer has not reported whether Sumtracker automates any of these steps, so the discussion remains open.
